questions.q: Why does the lesson say a review board cannot tell the difference between a tradeoff you overlooked and one you made deliberately just by looking at the diagram?
options: Because the architecture looks identical either way — the difference only shows up in what you say when it's questioned
Because review boards never look at diagrams during a review
Because deliberate tradeoffs are always drawn with a dashed line
Because overlooked gaps are illegal to include in a review deck
questions.explain: The diagram for a gap and the diagram for a deliberate, reasoned tradeoff can be identical — what distinguishes them is the stated reasoning behind the choice, not the architecture itself.

questions.q: What is the first step in the three-part pattern this lesson gives for defending a deliberate tradeoff?
options: Immediately propose rebuilding the design to remove the tradeoff
List every option ever considered, in full detail, from the start
Ask the review board to vote on whether the tradeoff is acceptable
Restate the actual constraint that drove the decision, before defending the choice itself
questions.explain: Naming the real constraint first reframes the conversation from "is this defensible in isolation" to "given this constraint, was this a reasonable call," which is the question a good reviewer actually wants answered.

questions.q: Why does the second step of the pattern call for naming the alternative and its specific cost in concrete terms?
options: Because vague cost estimates are more persuasive to a review board
Because the alternative must always be presented as impossible to build
Because it proves the more expensive option was considered and rejected for a reason, not unknown to the presenter
Because review boards require a signed cost estimate before any tradeoff can be discussed
questions.explain: Stating the alternative's concrete cost (e.g. infrastructure cost and engineering time) shows the board the more expensive option was actually weighed, rather than simply unknown to the presenter.

questions.q: What does "inviting the counter-proposal" accomplish, according to this lesson?
options: It shows the decision isn't held for its own sake, and puts the burden on the board to name what's actually changed rather than re-justifying a sound decision against vague discomfort
It signals the presenter has no confidence in the decision
It obligates the review board to immediately approve the design
It replaces the need to state the original constraint
questions.explain: Inviting the board to say what's changed shifts the conversation to concrete new information, rather than asking the presenter to defend a sound decision against a vague feeling that something might be wrong.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say that conceding every pushback to avoid conflict is not the same as being collaborative?
options: Because conceding to pushback is always the correct response in a review
Because collaboration means ignoring all feedback from the review board entirely
Because review boards are not allowed to push back on any tradeoff
Because agreeing to "reconsider" a sound decision just to end discomfort trains the room to treat every deliberate tradeoff as negotiable, undermining future defenses
questions.explain: Collaboration means engaging with genuinely new information when it's offered — abandoning a reasoned decision purely because it was questioned trains the room to treat all future tradeoffs as up for grabs.
